title: Control Plane Operator Handbook — TF primitives & upgrade sprint notes
content:
Purpose:
This is an operator-focused handbook for initializing, scaling, rotating, and upgrading the Redwood private control plane in VPC and on-prem environments. It collates the Terraform primitives we rely on, an upgrade sprint checklist used in Q4-2025, and pragmatic runbook steps for common rotation scenarios (KMS, TLS, instances). Aim is to be prescriptive enough for on-call engineers and light enough to stay editable during sprints.

Scope & audience:
- Audience: SREs, infra engineers running private control plane installs and Platform Engs who maintain TF modules.
- Scope: control-plane components (api-gw, controlplane-db, controlplane-api, controlplane-operator), network plumbing (VPCs, subnets, routes), secrets/KMS, certificates, and node scaling. Does NOT cover customer-app workloads or dedicated inference nodes.

Environment matrix (typical deployments we support):
- small: 3 control-plane nodes (2 masters, 1 replica), single-AZ VPC, 1x m60-equivalent GPU infra for inference (separate).
- medium: 5 control-plane nodes across 2 AZs, HA DB replica set, KMS in cloud HSM, load balancer per region.
- large: 7+ nodes, multi-AZ DB, multi-region routing with fallback.

Prerequisites (operator checklist before running tf apply):
- Terraform version pinned to 1.4.x in CI/runbook.
- Backend: S3/GCS bucket with state locking enabled (dynamodb/lock table).
- Access: operator has kms:Encrypt/Decrypt, iam:PassRole for instance profiles, and vault/KV write when relevant.
- Secrets: TLS certs and service-account keys staged in encrypted bucket or vault; KMS keys exist and are not scheduled for rotation during upgrades unless part of the plan.
- Monitoring: APM/tracing dashboards with baseline metrics captured (latency, error rate, control-plane CPU/ram, leader election metrics).

Terraform primitives (recommended minimal module surface):
- variables we expect to see in each env module (names used consistently across repos):
  - region (string)
  - azs (list of strings)
  - vpc_cidr (string)
  - public_subnets (list)
  - private_subnets (list)
  - control_plane_instance_type (string)
  - control_plane_desired_count (number)
  - ami_id (string)
  - tls_cert_s3_path (string)
  - kms_key_id (string)
  - db_instance_class (string)
  - db_storage_gb (number)

- outputs we rely on for orchestration:
  - control_plane_lb_dns
  - control_plane_instance_ids
  - control_plane_asg_name
  - db_endpoint
  - kms_key_arn

Module layout recommendations (primitives to keep stable):
- network/ (vpc, subnets, route tables) — mutate only for major network changes
- infra/ (load balancers, target groups, dns entries) — idempotent reconfigs OK
- controlplane/ (asg, instance user-data, autoscaling policies) — frequent changes here; design to be small and focused
- storage/ (rds, s3 buckets, backup policies) — careful with force-replace resources
- secrets/ (kms bindings, vault roles) — treat as separate, perform rotations with explicit steps

Sample terraform variable fragment (for operator copy/paste):

variable "control_plane_desired_count" {
  type    = number
  default = 3
  description = "Target control-plane node count (odd numbers preferred for leader election)"
}

variable "tls_cert_s3_path" {
  type = string
  description = "S3 path (or gs) to signed control-plane TLS bundle"
}

# When you need to set in CI: export TF_VAR_tls_cert_s3_path=s3://redwood-secrets/controlplane/prod/tls-bundle.pem

KMS rotation pattern (safe approach):
- Goal: rotate a CMK used to protect control-plane secrets with zero downtime for control-plane components.
- Constraints: cloud KMS does not automatically re-encrypt all dependent objects. We adopt a two-step rewrap pattern.

Steps:
1) Create new KMS key (alias e.g. alias/redwood/cp/rot-2026-02).
2) Update secrets manager wrapper (or Vault transit) to write new secrets encrypted under the new key while keeping old key as decryption fallback. Do NOT remove old key yet.
3) Roll control-plane components that read secrets (operator, api) one at a time: drain, replace instance with user-data that retrieves secrets using new key alias.
4) After verification period (48h), run bulk re-encrypt: fetch all secrets, re-encrypt with new key, write back. Use scripted API with concurrency limit (<=5).
5) Once all secrets rewrapped and all components read from new key, schedule retirement of old key after Key Rotation TTL (90 days recommended by compliance).

TLS cert rotation (internal API TLS) — non-disruptive flow:
- Prefer short-lived certs (90 days) signed by internal CA. Use cert bundles with full-chain in S3.
- Rotation steps:
  1) Generate cert and upload to tls_cert_s3_path-new.
  2) Add new cert path as secondary in config (feature flag in operator) so process can load both old and new during handshake phase.
  3) Roll nodes in ASG by reimaging or instance-terminate + auto-replace; new nodes will pick up new cert.
  4) After all nodes have the new cert, flip the primary alias and remove the old bundle after 24h.

Upgrade runway (major control plane version):
- Stage 0: Planning (1 week)
  - Define migration windows per customer region.
  - Run pre-upgrade upgrade-scan: terraform plan + diff of AMI changes, DB schema change scripts, dependency graph.
  - Smoke tests to add to CI for the upgrade (auth, leader election, API health endpoints).

- Stage 1: Canary (1 day)
  - Create 1-2 canary nodes in an isolated subset and point a small percentage (1-2%) of traffic via LB weight to them.
  - Run traffic generator for 2h with both read/write patterns. Observe error budgets.

- Stage 2: Rolling upgrade (4–8 hours depending on size)
  - Use smallest batch that keeps epochs stable (prefer 1 node at a time for small clusters; for larger clusters use 2 nodes).
  - Drain node, run post-start health probe (30s), verify metric parity vs baseline for 10m, then continue.
  - If leader election happens, validate applications gracefully accept new leader.

- Stage 3: Post-upgrade sweep (24–72h)
  - Confirm metrics, run full e2e smoke suite, and snapshot logs for analysis.
  - Update runbook with any manual fixes performed.

Rollback plan (if upgrade fails):
- If a canary fails: revert traffic weights and destroy canary nodes, revert the AMI in the TF variables, and block rollout.
- If rolling upgrade fails mid-way: pause, mark affected node images as tainted, restore from pre-upgrade AMI snapshot and re-attach. If DB migration was applied and is immutable, escalate to DB team — do not attempt blind schema rollback.
- Emergency rollback: restore cluster from last pre-upgrade backup snapshot into isolated VPC, cutover traffic once smoke tests pass. This is last-resort and will result in some data loss for writes after snapshot time.

Scaling and autoscaling knobs (practical rules):
- Target CPU for scale-out: 55% sustained for 10m (control-plane services are CPU sensitive).
- Min/Max nodes: keep min = odd number (3 or 5) for leader-election safety; max ≤ 2x expected steady state for predictable AZ placement.
- Use scale-in protection when running upgrades (disable automatic scale-in during rolling upgrades).
- Batching policy: apply gradual scale for spike – allow a 120s cool-down before additional scale-out.

Rotation scenarios quick-reference (command snippets & order):
- KMS rotate (safe): create -> update vault -> stagger node roll -> bulk rewrap -> retire old key.
- TLS rotate (safe): stage new bundle -> dual-load -> roll nodes -> flip -> remove old.
- Instance AMI roll: drain -> attach new AMI via ASG update -> health-check -> validate -> continue.

Validation checklist (post-change):
- control_plane_lb_dns resolves and returns 200 on /health for all AZs.
- leader_election_stable metric unchanged beyond 2x baseline spikes.
- replication lag (db) < 2s for normal traffic, < 5s during upgrade window for large clusters.
- backup job success within last 24h.
- Key metrics: API p50/p95 token-generation latency, DB connection count, pod restart counts.

Common failure modes & troubleshooting notes:
- symptom: leader flapping after restart -> likely clock skew, check NTP, and instance metadata.
- symptom: secrets decryption error -> confirm KMS policy includes new role, and check Vault transit logs.
- symptom: ASG not launching instances -> IAM role change or instance profile missing permissions; check EC2 quota and subnet IP exhaustion.

Incident playbook (fast path):
1) Triage: roll back LB weights to route traffic away from recent changes.
2) Isolate: scale up healthy nodes if capacity allows and mark suspect nodes as draining.
3) Telemetry: collect control-plane logs (last 1h), and export to S3 with tagging "incident-<timestamp>".
4) If rollback necessary, follow Rollback plan section.

Postmortem & notes for next sprint:
- Capture specific TF resources that required manual touches. Keep a short list (resource id, reason) appended to the PR for the tf-module repo.
- Add failing smoke tests to CI, and a canary test monitoring alert for 24h post-rollout.

Operational run-commands (examples):
- terraform plan: terraform plan -var-file=env/prod.tfvars -lock=true
- drain node: aws ec2 terminate-instances --instance-ids i-0123abcd --region us-west-2 (ASG will replace).
- rewrap secrets (example script): ./scripts/rewrap-secrets --src-key alias/redwood/cp/old --dst-key alias/redwood/cp/new --concurrency 3

On-call contacts & ownership:
- Primary: eng-oncall-private (pager)
- Secondary: Maya Thompson (pager escalate contact), Priya Nair (backup)
- DB escalation: Luis Ortega

Open items / TODOs (tracking for next upgrade sprint):
- Add explicit terraform checks that fail fast on db.force_replace in plans.
- Create a smoke generator job that mirrors write-heavy customer patterns for canaries.
- Automate cert dual-load support in control-plane operator (feature flag).

Notes (editorial):
- This handbook is intentionally compact; keep procedural steps as single-line bullets when possible so on-call can quickly scan.
- When editing, update the linked artifacts list and append a short changelog entry at the top with date and author.
